name: Shave to thicken myth

lead: Men with patchy beards sometimes shave the area, believing hair will return thicker, darker or faster and even things out.

Wikipedia reports that shaving does not change terminal hair thickness, coarseness or darkness. Sources attribute the impression of thicker hair to blunt-cut tips, the stiffness of short hair, sun-lightened longer hair and age-related changes.

paras: People shave the thin area clean and watch regrowth over the following weeks. The blunt stubble can look and feel denser at first, which is the effect commonly noted.
No harms are specific to the belief; ordinary shaving irritation can occur.

chain: Hair seems thicker or more even
angle.text: The idea is that shaving a patchy area makes hair return thicker, darker or faster, evening out the beard. Published sources report shaving does not change the hair; short blunt-tipped regrowth can just look denser.

lead: The belief that shaving makes hair grow back thicker, darker or faster is a long-circulating grooming idea. It shows up in beard-growth circles, where some men shave patchy cheeks or a thin chin area in the hope that the regrowth will come in denser and fill the beard out, and in body-hair grooming generally.

Wikipedia's article on shaving states that shaving does not cause terminal hair to grow back thicker, coarser or darker, and lists reasons the impression arises.[1] The idea therefore sits in the wiki as a looksmaxxing belief with no published controlled trial behind it, while the grooming implications are practical: how a shaved area looks as it regrows, and how beard density develops over time.[1][2]
infobox: Shaving increases hair thickness or growth rate
Shaving does not make terminal hair thicker, coarser or darker[1]
Androgens such as DHT; rate partly genetic[2]

paras: Proponents of the idea hold that cutting hair at the surface stimulates the follicle, producing denser or coarser regrowth. Some beard-growers apply it to cheek patches, shaving the area in the hope that it fills in.

Wikipedia describes several reasons given for the perception. Hair that has never been cut ends in a natural taper, whereas cut hair has a blunt tip and can look thicker and feel coarser.[1] Short hairs are stiffer than long ones, and unshaven hair may be lightened by sun exposure, so regrowth can look darker by contrast.[1]

The article also notes that hair generally becomes coarser and spreads to more areas with age, so a teenager who begins shaving around 16 may attribute later maturation changes to shaving.[1] Facial hair growth is described as driven by androgens including dihydrotestosterone from puberty onward, and growth rate is partly genetic.[2]
The Wikipedia section on this topic cites a Mayo Clinic page, a Snopes entry and an NIH MedlinePlus page on age-related hair changes rather than a controlled trial of regrowth.[1]

A T Nation thread on hairless men shows how beard development is discussed: one poster says he was naturally somewhat hairless yet still got a decent beard, that his full beard did not arrive until his thirties and was still thickening at nearly 36, while a friend had a full thick beard at 14.[3] Another thread poster suggests that a chinstrap beard that is too narrow can be shaved off or thickened up.[4]

lore.intro: Beard-growth discussions commonly treat facial hair thickness as developing with age and genetics, and shaving to thicken is one tactic raised for patchy beards.[3]
